tools.name: search_guidelines
tools.description:
Look a rule up in the UMR guidelines (umr4nlp/umr-guidelines, guidelines.md).

keywords: terms to look for, e.g. "aspect", "modal strength", "have-rel-role-92", ":quant",
"reentrancy". Passages with more of the keywords come first, then those whose heading has
them, then those that mention them most.
max_results: how many passages to return (at most 10).

Returns {"sections": [{"heading": the passage's place in the guidelines ("Part 3. ... > Part
3-3-1. Aspect"), "text": the passage (a section, or a part of a long one)}], "found": how
many passages matched}.

tools.name: propbank_lookup
tools.description:
Look up a lemma and every alternate of it in PropBank (at most 20 per call).

language is "en" or "zh". Returns Markdown: per lemma, every roleset with its roles and all
its examples (the sentence, then each argument; traces such as *T*-1 are PropBank's own),
or "not in PropBank". Lemmas over the limit are not looked up: the last line names them
(call again with them). There is no PropBank for another language (Uzbek): nothing.

tools.name: search_annotations
tools.description:
Find how a case is annotated: gold UMR annotations of whole sentences.

language: "zh" (Chinese) or "en" (English).
keywords: words or pieces to look for, matched anywhere in a sentence or its annotation:
words of the text (e.g. "发生", "wanted to"), concepts ("have-org-role-91", "identity-91"),
roles (":ARG1-of", ":manner"), attribute values (":aspect state"). Sentences with more of the
keywords come first.
max_results: how many gold sentences to return (at most 10).

Returns {"gold": [{"doc", "sentence_number", "sentence", "annotation"}], where annotation is
the sentence's whole annotation (words, sentence-level graph, alignment, document-level
annotation); "found": how many gold sentences matched in all}.

## Input

Language: en
Document: en-0008, sentence 6 of 9

The sentence: its number, a tab, then its words separated by spaces.

6	He will spend the next several days at the medical center there before he returns home with his wife Sherry .

content.content:
## spend

### spend-01 (use money, paying money/time)

- ARG0: spender, buyer
- ARG1: thing bought, commodity
- ARG2: seller
- ARG3: price paid, money
- ARG4: benefactive

Example 1 (demonstrating commodity and price): The NIH currently spends about $8 million annually on fetal-tissue research.
- ARG0: The NIH
- ARGM-TMP: currently
- ARG3: about $8 million
- ARGM-TMP: annually
- ARG1: on fetal-tissue research.
- rel: spends

Example 2 (with TMP): They spent $325,000 in 1989.
- ARG0: They
- ARG3: $325,000
- ARGM-TMP: in 1989
- rel: spent

Example 3 (arg0): Government spending is actually increasing .
- ARG0: Government
- rel: spending

Example 4 (arg 0, 1 and 3): The question is whether his spending $7.7 million on food, drink, hotels and parties is excessive.
- ARG0: his
- ARG3: $7.7 million
- ARG1: on food, drink, hotels and parties
- rel: spending

### spend-02 (bide time)

- ARG0: bider, waiter
- ARG1: unit of time
- ARG2: activity

Example 1 (spend time): He spends his days *trace-1* sketching passers-by or *trace-2* trying to.
- ARG0: He
- ARG1: his days
- ARG2: *trace-1* sketching passers-by or *trace-2* trying to.
- rel: spends

Example 2 (simpler example): Mr. Bernstein has spent much of his time in recent years on human rights issues.
- ARG0: Mr. Bernstein
- ARG1: much of his time
- ARGM-TMP: in recent years
- ARG2: on human rights issues.
- rel: spent

### spend-04 (be used up)

- ARG1: thing used up
- ARG2: cause

Example 1 (arg 1 only - most common): the spent fuel rod
- ARG1: fuel rod
- rel: spent

Example 2 (with arg 2): Man! I am completely spent from that basketball game!
- ARGM-DIS: Man!
- ARG1: I
- ARGM-EXT: completely
- ARG2: from that basketball game
- rel: spent

Example 3 (adjectival): The shampoo and conditioner are completely spent.
- ARG1: The shampoo and conditioner
- ARGM-EXT: completely
- rel: spent.

## return

### return-01 (come back)

- ARG1: entity in motion
- ARG2: (extent -- rare)
- ARG3: start point
- ARG4: end point
- ARGM: medium

Example 1 (typical): I-1 need *trace*-1 to return on Tuesday.
- ARG1: *trace*
- ARGM-TMP: on Tuesday
- rel: return

Example 2 (metaphorical): Parents are returning to the cloth diaper.
- ARG1: Parents
- ARG4: to the cloth diaper
- rel: returning

Example 3 (Example of end point as 'return to ..."): they expect a return to full operations by Saturday
- ARG4: to full operations
- ARGM-TMP: by Saturday
- rel: return

Example 4 (Example with arg 1 and 4): their return to black townships across the country
- ARG1: their
- ARG4: to black townships across the country
- rel: return

Example 5 (Example with args 0 and 4): their return to Earth
- ARG1: their
- ARG4: to Earth
- rel: return

Example 6 (Example with arg 1): The possible return of the verification team
- ARG1: of the verification team
- rel: return

Example 7 (revert to): a return to Soviet-era symbolism in Russia
- ARG4: to Soviet-era symbolism in Russia
- rel: return

### return-02 (give back)

- ARG0: giver
- ARG1: thing given
- ARG2: entity given to

Example 1 (Japanese baseball): Fans politely return foul balls to stadium ushers.
- ARG0: Fans
- ARGM-MNR: politely
- ARG1: foul balls
- ARG2: to stadium ushers
- rel: return

Example 2 (seeking comment): Charles LaBella didn't return phone calls seeking comment.
- ARG0: Charles LaBella
- ARGM-NEG: n't
- ARG1: phone calls seeking comment
- rel: return

Example 3 (Example with all args): his return toast to Mr. Nixon
- ARG0: his
- ARG1: toast
- ARG2: to Mr. Nixon
- rel: return

Example 4 (Example with args 1 and 2): the return of cheaper shares to the lender
- ARG1: of cheaper shares
- ARG2: to the lender
- rel: return

Example 5 (Example with all args): Their return of our refugees to their homes
- ARG0: Their
- ARG1: of our refugees
- ARG2: to their homes
- rel: return

Example 6 (Possibly confusing use): Jack's safe return
- ARG1: Jack's
- ARGM-MNR: safe
- rel: return

Example 7 (Args 1 and 2): The return of East Jerusalem to the Palestinians
- ARG1: of East Jerusalem
- ARG2: to the Palestinians
- rel: return

### return-03 (bring back)

- ARG0: entity bring something back
- ARG1: thing brought back
- ARG2: attribute of arg1, state arg1 is brought back to

Example 1 (transitive active): The company had returned the plant to routine inspection in August.
- ARG0: The company
- ARG1: the plant
- ARG2: to routine inspection
- ARGM-TMP: in August
- rel: returned

Example 2 (Example with arg 1): the best punt return , quarterback sack , etc
- ARG1: punt
- rel: return

Example 3 (Example with arg 0 and arg 1): The mechine's ball return was broken.
- ARG0: The mechine's
- ARG1: ball
- rel: return

### return-04 (send back)

- ARG0: sender
- ARG1: thing sent
- ARG2: sent-to

Example 1 (all args): Mr. Koskotas is fighting extradition proceedings that [*T*-2] would return him to Greece, where he is charged with embezzling more than $250 million from the Bank of Crete.
- ARG0: [*T*-2]
- ARGM-RCL: that -> extradition proceedings
- ARGM-MOD: would
- ARG1: him
- ARG2: to Greece, where he is charged with embezzling more than $250 million from the Bank of Crete
- rel: return

### return-05 (exchange, trade)

- ARG0: agent, entity trading
- ARG1: theme
- ARG2: other exchanger
- ARG3: secondary theme

Example 1 (Args 1,3): North Korea agreed to dismantle its nuclear program in return for economic aid.
- ARG1: for economic aid
- ARG3: North Korea agreed to dismantle its nuclear program
- rel: return

Example 2 (Example with args 1): in return for removing all our tariff barriers
- ARG1: for removing all our tariff barriers
- rel: return

Example 3 (Often in the form of 'in return for'): In return for services rendered
- ARG1: for services rendered
- rel: return

Example 4 (It is rare to find this with more than arg 1): In return for your patience
- ARG1: for your patience
- rel: return

### return-06 (give a dividend)

- ARG0: thing providing a dividend
- ARG1: dividend, earnings
- ARG2: recipient

Example 1 (Monitary example (usual use)): a 0.89 % return on assets for Security Pacific
- ARG1: 0.89 %
- ARG0: on assets
- ARG2: for Security Pacific
- rel: return

Example 2 (the return percentage can be 'earnings'): KKR racked up annual returns of 60 % in the three years it owned Storer .
- ARGM-TMP: annual
- ARG1: of 60 %
- rel: returns

Example 3 (Non-monitary example): Returns from just under a third of the polling stations
- ARG0: from just under a third of the polling stations
- rel: Returns

Example 4 (Arg 0 is often inanimate): A return of investments of 32%
- ARG0: on investments
- ARG1: of 32%
- rel: return

Example 5 (Animate arg 2): whose returns after tax have trailed tuition increases
- ARG2: whose
- ARGM-TMP: after tax
- rel: returns

In order to assess whether one or two concepts should be identified for UMR annotation, unity under negation is chosen as a criterion. In English Causatives, for instance, negation can apply to the causing event and to the caused event separately as in (1), indicating that the causing event and the caused event are construed as independent predicates. Therefore, a "cause"-event is identified in addition to the "drink"-event expressed by the verb root. 3-1-3-2 (1) 3-1-3-2 (1a) Grandmother made the kid drink the water. ``` (d/ drink :cause (m/ make :actor (p/ person :ARG1-of (h/ have-rel-role-92 :ARG3 (g/ grandmother)) :ref-number Singular) :aspect Performance :modstr FullAff) :actor (k2/ kid :ref-number Singular) :undergoer (w/ water) :aspect Performance :modstr FullAff) ``` 3-1-3-2 (1b) Grandmother did not make the kid drink the water. ``` (d/ drink :cause (m/ make :actor (p/ person :ARG1-of (h/ have-rel-role-92 :ARG3 (g/ grandmother)) :ref-number Singular) :aspect Performance :modstr FullNeg) :actor (k2/ kid :ref-number Singular) :undergoer (w/ water) :aspect Performance :modstr NeutAff) ``` 3-1-3-2 (1c) Grandmother made the kid not drink the water. ``` (d/ drink :cause (m/ make :actor (p/ person :ARG1-of (h/ have-rel-role-92 :ARG3 (g/ grandmother)) :ref-number Singular) :aspect Performance :modstr FullAff) :actor (k2/ kid :ref-number Singular) :undergoer (w/ water) :aspect Performance :modstr FullNeg) ``` Kukama (Tupían), on the other hand, has a morphological causative, as in (2).
